331.quote_or_event: “The world and its affairs are totally false; know this well, my friend. Says Nanak, it is like a wall of sand; it shall not endure.”
331.explanation: In his saloks Guru Tegh Bahadur warns that everything built in the world is as unstable as a wall of sand, and that recognising this is the beginning of wisdom.
331.tie_back: The Kural calls it the lowest folly to take passing things for permanent; Guru Tegh Bahadur urges us to know clearly that the world's affairs will not endure.
331.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1429, Salok Mahala 9, Salok 49, Guru Tegh Bahadur (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
331._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one on the error of trusting what is impermanent; 'false' here means perishable rather than unreal.

332.quote_or_event: “That wealth, which he believes to be his own, in an instant, belongs to another.”
332.explanation: Guru Tegh Bahadur observes how quickly possessions that seem securely one's own pass to someone else.
332.tie_back: The Kural pictures great wealth arriving like a gathering crowd and leaving like the crowd after the show; Guru Tegh Bahadur makes the same point about how suddenly wealth departs.
332.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1008, Raag Maaroo, Guru Tegh Bahadur (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
332._accuracy_note: A strong fit on the sudden departure of wealth, without the Kural's theatrical image of a crowd assembling and dispersing.

333.quote_or_event: “One who works for what he eats, and gives some of what he has”
333.explanation: Guru Nanak names the person who earns honestly and shares part of it as the one who knows the true path; this is the Sikh pillar of vand chhakna, sharing one's earnings.
333.tie_back: The Kural says that since wealth does not stay, it should be used at once for good deeds that last; Guru Nanak likewise points the householder's wealth towards giving.
333.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1245, Raag Saarang, Saarang ki Vaar, Salok, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
333._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: the verse commends sharing what one earns, but does not argue from the instability of wealth or urge giving at once, as the Kural does.

334.quote_or_event: “Day by day, hour by hour, life runs its course, and the body withers away.”
334.explanation: Kabir describes life being whittled away unit by unit of time, days into watches and watches into hours, until the body is spent.
334.tie_back: The Kural unmasks the day as a saw that cuts away at life; Kabir sees the same steady erosion of life in each passing day and hour.
334.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 692, Raag Dhanaasree, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
334._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one on time as the gradual consumer of life; only the saw image itself is missing.

335.quote_or_event: “Kabeer, that which you have to do tomorrow - do it today instead; and that which you have to do now - do it immediately! Later on, you will not be able to do anything, when death hangs over your head.”
335.explanation: Kabir urges the seeker to stop postponing what matters, because once death arrives the chance to act is gone.
335.tie_back: The Kural says to hurry to do good before the tongue is stilled and the death rattle comes; Kabir gives the same urgent counsel not to wait until death is upon us.
335.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1371, Salok Bhagat Kabir, Salok 138 (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
335._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one; Sikh commentators read the deed Kabir has in mind chiefly as remembrance of God, where the Kural speaks of good deeds generally.

336.quote_or_event: “Whatever has been created shall be destroyed; everyone shall perish, today or tomorrow.”
336.explanation: Guru Tegh Bahadur states the universal law that all that is born must pass, the only question being whether it is today or tomorrow.
336.tie_back: The Kural ironically praises the world's 'greatness', that one who was here yesterday is gone today; Guru Tegh Bahadur states the same sudden passing as a plain law.
336.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1429, Salok Mahala 9, Salok 52, Guru Tegh Bahadur (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
336._accuracy_note: A strong fit on the suddenness of death, without the Kural's ironic 'greatness'.

337.quote_or_event: “The self-willed manmukhs make their calculations and plans, but only the actions of the Creator come to pass.”
337.explanation: Guru Nanak contrasts the endless schemes of the self-centred person with the reality that events unfold by the Creator's will (hukam).
337.tie_back: The Kural mocks those who cannot be sure of one more moment yet make countless plans; Guru Nanak likewise sets human plan-making against our real powerlessness over what will happen.
337.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 60, Siree Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
337._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: the futility of plans is shared, but Guru Nanak grounds it in divine will rather than in the uncertainty of one's next moment of life.

338.quote_or_event: “When the soul-swan flies away, by the Command of the Lord, her dust mingles with dust.”
338.explanation: Guru Nanak pictures death as the soul, imagined as a swan, flying off at God's command while the body it leaves behind returns to dust.
338.tie_back: The Kural compares the bond of body and soul to a bird leaving its egg or nest empty behind it; Guru Nanak uses the same image of a bird flying from an abandoned body.
338.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1111, Raag Tukhaari, Chhant, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
338._accuracy_note: A strong fit, sharing the bird-leaving-its-shelter image; the Kural stresses how slight the bond was, while Guru Nanak stresses God's command.

339.quote_or_event: “Death would not be called bad, O people, if one knew how to truly die.”
339.explanation: In the Alahanian, his hymns of mourning, Guru Nanak teaches that death is not to be dreaded by one who has learned to die to ego while living.
339.tie_back: The Kural makes death as natural as falling asleep and birth as waking; Guru Nanak likewise strips death of its terror, though by a different route.
339.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 579, Raag Vadhans, Alahanian, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
339._accuracy_note: Next-best only: both make death less fearsome, but Gurbani does not use the sleep-and-waking image here, and 'truly dying' means dying to ego, not the natural cycle the Kural describes.

340.quote_or_event: “Burn away your hopes and desires, and live like a guest in this world.”
340.explanation: Guru Amar Das counsels living in the world as a visitor who knows the stay is temporary, not as an owner settling in for good.
340.tie_back: The Kural wonders whether the soul, lodging for a while in the body, has yet found a permanent home; Guru Amar Das likewise teaches that here we are only guests.
340.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 646, Raag Sorath (Sorath ki Vaar, salok), Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
340._accuracy_note: A strong thematic fit on temporary lodging; Gurbani speaks of the person as a guest in the world rather than the soul as a lodger in the body.
